references.text: Jesus stopped and commanded that the blind man be brought to him. This shows Jesus' attention to those who call out to him in faith. In the parallel account in [ref:Mark 10:49|Mark 10:49], the blind man is called to Jesus with the words, "Be of good cheer, arise! He is calling you."

In [ref:Matt 20:32|Matt 20:32] the parallel account is told where Jesus stopped and called out to the blind men and asked what they wanted him to do for them, following the same pattern: Jesus stops, calls them to himself, and asks.

In [ref:Luk 7:44|Luke 7:44], Jesus stops and turns toward the woman who had anointed his feet, speaking to Simon. Luke uses a similar approach where Jesus pauses and gives his attention to someone seeking him.

The context in [ref:Luk 18:35-39|Luke 18:35–39] shows that the blind man at Jericho cried out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" despite the crowd trying to silence him. It is this cry that causes Jesus to stop.

The continuation in [ref:Luk 18:41-42|Luke 18:41–42] shows Jesus' question, "What do you want me to do for you?" and the healing. Verse 40 is the transition where Jesus takes the initiative to meet the blind man's faith.
In [ref:Luk 8:44-47|Luke 8:44–47], Jesus stops and seeks out the woman who touched him in the crowd. Here too, Jesus shows personal attention amid a multitude and calls the believer to himself.

In [ref:Mark 10:49-50|Mark 10:49–50] it is described that Jesus stopped and said, "Call him here!", and Bartimaeus threw off his cloak, jumped up, and came to Jesus. Mark's account gives further details about the same event.

[ref:Jes 55:6|Isaiah 55:6] urges: "Seek the Lord while he may be found; call on him while he is near." The blind man's cry and Jesus' response—that he stops and calls him to himself—is a living illustration of this prophetic word.
